heading: Canine Babesiosis: Supporting Oxygen Delivery During the Critical Treatment Window
lead: A retrospective veterinary R&D case involving a critically ill shepherd dog with babesiosis-associated severe anemia and no donor blood available. The corrected timeline compares 5 November 2026 before BHOC with 7 November 2026 after two administrations.

paragraphs.text: The dog presented in critical condition with babesiosis and severe anemia. Donor blood was not available. According to the supplied case account, BHOC oxygen-carrier support was administered twice, with approximately 14 hours between administrations.

The CBC on 5 November 2026 was obtained before BHOC support: HGB 43 g/L, RBC 1.59 ×10¹²/L and HCT 10.6%. On 7 November 2026, after two BHOC administrations, follow-up values were HGB 85 g/L, RBC 3.7 ×10¹²/L and HCT 23.9%. This was the third calendar day of the reported sequence, not a comparison between two unspecified samples.

The clinical objective was to support oxygen-carrying function during the critical treatment window, giving the veterinarian time to treat the underlying babesiosis and the animal time to stabilize and recover. BHOC was not being used as treatment for the parasite itself.
We believe that in canine babesiosis, the primary clinical need is not donor blood itself, but effective oxygen-delivery support during the critical phase of the disease.

Babesiosis destroys red blood cells and can rapidly compromise tissue oxygenation. In this situation, the immediate therapeutic objective should be to support the patient’s oxygen-carrying capacity, maintain tissue oxygen delivery, and create a treatment window in which the veterinarian can control the underlying infection.

Our view is that, in selected cases, temporary oxygenation support may reduce or even avoid the need for donor blood, while giving the animal time to stabilize, respond to antiparasitic treatment, and begin its own recovery process.

In addition to the intended oxygen-delivery support, the follow-up records show an increase in the measured red blood cell count, hematocrit and hemoglobin. This raises the research question of whether BHOC support may also contribute to erythropoietic recovery and new red blood cell formation. That is a hypothesis for investigation, not a demonstrated product effect: these two CBCs alone do not establish increased red-cell production or identify the cause of the changes.
The goal is not simply to replace blood volume. The goal is to support the function that matters most at that moment: oxygen delivery.
Support oxygenation. Stabilize the patient. Give the veterinarian time to treat the disease. Give the animal time to heal.

A historical prospective randomized clinical trial in 12 dogs naturally infected with Babesia rossi compared Oxyglobin (hemoglobin glutamer-200) with packed red blood cells and reported similar overall improvements in blood-gas, acid-base and blood-pressure measures, with some clinical measures normalizing more rapidly after packed cells. This historical HBOC evidence does not establish BHOC efficacy or a universal transfusion-avoidance protocol.

newsSummary: A shepherd-dog babesiosis case compares CBC before BHOC on 5 Nov 2026 with follow-up on 7 Nov after two administrations. HGB rose from 43 to 85 g/L, RBC from 1.59 to 3.7 ×10¹²/L and HCT from 10.6% to 23.9%. The case infographic shows the corrected timeline; possible erythropoietic effects remain a research hypothesis.

context: This page describes an individual investigational veterinary R&D case. It does not establish causality, regulatory approval, a universal treatment protocol, or that donor blood should never be used in babesiosis.

The observed increase in RBC, HCT and HGB occurred between the baseline CBC on 5 November and the follow-up CBC on 7 November, after two BHOC administrations and treatment of the underlying disease. A possible contribution to erythropoiesis is hypothesis-generating; the supplied comparison does not establish a direct effect on new red blood cell production.
Transfusion decisions remain clinical decisions for the treating veterinarian. This account is not a recommendation to withhold an indicated transfusion.

The supplied case photographs and laboratory records were provided by Archil Jaliashvili. The approved infographic illustrates the reported chronology and values; it is separate from the original laboratory records.
